National prevalence estimates for early warning indicators (EWIs) of HIV drug resistance can be calculated by combining data from randomly sampled clinics and conveniently sampled clinics. This approach allows for representative data collection while progressively scaling up monitoring to include all clinics in a country. Random sampling enables countries to calculate a national aggregate prevalence estimate for each EWI. Conveniently available data from certain clinics can also be incorporated without compromising representativeness. Primary sampling refers to the selection of clinics, while secondary sampling involves selecting patients within a clinic. Ideally, all antiretroviral therapy (ART) clinics in a country should report on EWIs of HIV drug resistance. In cases where this is not feasible, countries are encouraged to progressively expand EWI reporting using a multi-year scale-up approach. For example, a country may begin by sampling 20% of clinics in the first year, then expand coverage by an additional 20% each year until all clinics are included by the fifth year. Clinics can be selected using a combination of convenience sampling and random sampling, with results summarized in a nationally representative manner through weighting. Clinics with historical EWI reporting or readily available data, such as those with electronic medical records (EMRs), should always be included in the sample. Representative sampling of clinics can be achieved through simple random sampling or stratified random sampling. If stratified random sampling is used, it is recommended to limit stratification to one level, such as district or province. For example, in Year 1, a country may monitor EWIs at five clinics with readily available data and four randomly sampled clinics. In subsequent years, additional clinics are randomly sampled to expand EWI monitoring until all clinics are included by Year 5. After Year 5, all clinics continue to report EWIs annually. Data abstraction for EWIs should ideally rely on a census of patient-level data, meaning data for all eligible patients. If a census is not possible, systematic or simple random sampling of patient records within a clinic can be used to achieve results generalizable to the entire eligible population at the clinic. The sample size required for secondary sampling depends on the size of the eligible patient population, which varies by EWI. For example, the eligible population for ART adherence proxy (on-time ARV drug pick-up) includes all eligible pediatric patients receiving ART at the clinic, while the eligible population for viral load suppression includes adult patients on ART for at least six months with a viral load test result available. Sample size calculations are designed to achieve 95% confidence intervals with a margin of error of ±7%. Clinics must randomly sample patient records until the required sample size is reached, and records with missing or incomplete data should not be excluded. WHO provides an Excel-based EWI data abstraction tool to facilitate data collection and classification. Clinics with more than 30% missing data for a specific indicator are assigned a grey score, indicating insufficient data for analysis. After data abstraction, each clinic calculates the EWIs and assigns appropriate classifications (red, amber, green, or grey) based on performance thresholds. A grey classification is used when 30% or more of the required data is missing. Nationally, countries should report the proportions of clinics achieving each classification for each indicator and for both adult and pediatric populations. This information can be presented in a scorecard format to help program managers identify areas needing improvement and monitor progress over time. At the national level, aggregate prevalence estimates for each EWI can be calculated by combining data from all sampled clinics. Weighting is applied to account for clinic size, ensuring that clinics with larger patient populations contribute more to the national estimate. However, aggregation should not be performed if less than 70% of data is available for the nationally eligible population monitored by a specific indicator. A flowchart is provided to assess the feasibility of data aggregation at the national level. Data abstraction can be performed using paper-based or electronic medical records (EMRs). If paper-based records are used, clinic staff trained in the national EWI monitoring strategy should abstract data retrospectively, typically once per year. If EMRs are in place, national program experts should guide the data abstraction process. Clinics with more than 30% missing data for a specific indicator should be classified as grey. Data reliability refers to the accuracy of data abstracted for each indicator, while data completeness addresses the proportion of missing information. Clinics with less than 70% available data for any indicator should report a grey score, signaling the need for support in record-keeping. Data consistency involves evaluating the alignment of patient information across different record systems within the same clinic. Inconsistencies or incompleteness in data often indicate systemic issues in record-keeping that should be addressed to improve patient monitoring systems and clinic practices.
